column16: A coastal hyperarid desert along the Atlantic coast of southern Africa, with sand seas, gravel plains and very little rain. Its dryness, wind-shaped landforms and sparse microbial life make it a long-standing analog for Martian deserts. The marker is a generic regional point, not a specific field site.

column16: Large star and linear dunes of the Namib Sand Sea surround Sossusvlei, a clay pan that floods only in rare wet years. Wind-built dune fields like this are compared with Martian dune fields, which are also shaped by wind in a very dry setting. Caveat: Martian dunes are mostly basaltic sand while Namib sand is mostly quartz, so the analogy is about dune form and wind processes rather than composition.

column4: Central Namib, north of the Kuiseb River, Namibia
column16: Hyperarid gravel plains north of the Kuiseb River near the Gobabeb research station, where mean annual rainfall is only about 20 mm and coastal fog is a key source of moisture. Cyanobacteria living under translucent quartz pebbles (hypoliths) are studied by NASA-affiliated researchers as a model for how life might survive in dry Martian soils. The photo shows the Gobabeb station with the desert behind it, not the exact marker point.

column16: The largest ice-free region of Antarctica: cold, extremely dry valleys swept by katabatic winds, with permafrost, salts and patterned ground. Together these make it one of the closest Earth analogs to the cold, dry surface of Mars. The marker is a generic regional point.

column4: South Fork, upper Wright Valley, McMurdo Dry Valleys, Antarctica
column16: A small, very shallow pond in upper Wright Valley and one of the saltiest natural water bodies on Earth; its calcium-chloride brine stays liquid far below 0 °C. Because liquid water on Mars today could only exist briefly as cold brines, the pond is used as an analog for how such brines might form, for example by salts absorbing water vapour. column16: One of the coldest and driest of the McMurdo Dry Valleys, its floor covered in polygonal patterned ground. Under a thin layer of rock debris lies buried glacier ice that has been estimated at up to about 8 million years old (the age is debated). Polygons, sublimation and debris-covered ice make it a classic analog for ice-rich terrain on Mars.

column16: An impact crater about 20 km across in the polar desert of Devon Island; its age is often quoted as about 23 million years, though later studies argue it is older (TODO: check the current age estimate). Since 1997 the Haughton-Mars Project has used its cold, dry, rocky terrain, impact geology and permafrost to rehearse Mars exploration. It has also served lunar studies: in 2007 NASA's K10 rovers ran lunar-analog site surveys here.

column16: The interior of Devon Island, often called the largest uninhabited island on Earth, is a barren, rocky polar plateau with permafrost and patterned ground. The lack of vegetation, broken rocky terrain and low sun angles make it useful for rehearsing lunar-style surface operations; NASA's 2007 K10 rover surveys near Haughton Crater were run as lunar analog tests. column16: A high-Arctic polar desert on western Ellesmere Island, next to the Eureka weather station at about 80° N, with very little precipitation, continuous permafrost and ground ice. Months of polar night and a sun that stays low even in midsummer give lighting loosely comparable to the lunar polar regions. column4: South shore of Mistastin Lake, Labrador, Canada
column16: Mistastin is an impact structure about 28 km across, formed roughly 36–38 million years ago in a target that includes anorthosite, the plagioclase-rich rock that makes up the lunar highlands. On the south shore of the lake, fractured anorthosite target rock and breccias packed with anorthosite fragments are exposed right at the water's edge; more anorthosite occurs on the central island (the crater's central uplift). This lunar-like target is why Mistastin is studied as an analog for highland craters on the Moon.

column4: Southwest rim of Mistastin Lake, Labrador, Canada
column16: Discovery Hill is a ramp-shaped butte on the southwestern rim terrace of Mistastin Lake, capped by the crater's thickest impact-melt rock (about 80 m in most studies) with columnar cooling joints. Zircon in its black melt glass records temperatures above about 2370 °C, among the highest known for any rock at Earth's surface. Because the melted target was largely anorthositic, the hill is an analog for lunar highland impact melts, and it hosted the CSA-funded 'Impacts: Lunar Sample Return' analog mission, a simulated crewed lunar exploration.

Reported melt thickness varies by source: 80 m (Marion 2009; Mader 2015), 85 m (Tolometti et al. 2020), 120 m (Mader & Osinski 2015 abstract)

column16: A crater about 45 km across on the western edge of Isidis Planitia that held a lake billions of years ago; a river delta is preserved on its western side. NASA's Perseverance rover has explored it since 2021, searching for signs of ancient microbial life and collecting samples.

column16: A crater about 21 km across almost exactly at the lunar south pole. Its floor is permanently shadowed and may trap water ice, while parts of its rim get sunlight for much of the year, making the area a candidate region for Artemis landings.

column16: A mountain about 5 km high roughly 120 km from the lunar south pole. Its summit has long sunlit periods and frequent line of sight to Earth, so it is studied as a site for communications and as a candidate Artemis landing region.
